title: Covalent bonding
examples: How do I know if a bond is covalent or ionic?
Can you show me how to draw a molecule with more than two atoms?
What is the difference between a single and a double bond?

explain.say: Today we are learning about covalent bonding between atoms. A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons with each other. This sharing allows the atoms to become stable. We will look at how many pairs of electrons they share.

A single bond means that two atoms are sharing exactly one pair of electrons. For example, in a molecule of hydrogen gas, two hydrogen atoms share one pair. This sharing keeps the two atoms stuck together.
Sometimes atoms share more than one pair of electrons. This creates a double bond between the two atoms. Think about oxygen gas; it has two shared pairs of electrons. This makes the bond stronger.
Atoms can even share three pairs of electrons in a triple bond. Nitrogen gas is a common example of this. It shares three pairs to achieve a stable structure. This is quite a lot of sharing.
In a molecule like carbon dioxide, the carbon atom shares electrons with two oxygen atoms. The carbon forms double bonds with each oxygen. This shows how sharing works in larger molecules.

In everyday life, when you mix baking soda and vinegar, they react to form carbon dioxide gas. This gas is held together by covalent bonds between the carbon and oxygen atoms. The bonds are what keep the gas molecule together.

faq.q: What is the difference between covalent and ionic bonds?
faq.a: In covalent bonding, electrons are shared between atoms. In ionic bonding, one atom transfers electrons to another atom. You might also ask: 'Does sharing mean they are neutral?' or 'How do I tell them apart?'
asks: Are covalent bonds sharing or stealing?
What is the difference between sharing and transferring electrons?

faq.q: Do all molecules have covalent bonds?
faq.a: Most molecules formed between non-metal atoms have covalent bonds. Atoms tend to share electrons to achieve a stable outer shell. You could also ask: 'Can metals form covalent bonds?' or 'Are all compounds covalent?'

faq.q: How do I draw the number of bonds correctly?
faq.a: You must draw one pair for a single bond, two pairs for a double bond, and three pairs for a triple bond. Remember that the total number of valence electrons must be accounted for. Another way to ask this is: 'How many lines for a double bond?'
asks: What does the number of lines mean?
If I have four bonds, what is that?

faq.q: What is the octet rule in this context?
faq.a: The octet rule suggests that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to have eight electrons in their outer shell. This makes them chemically stable. You might also ask: 'Why do atoms want eight electrons?'
asks: What is the goal of bonding?
How many electrons do atoms try to have?

faq.q: Can a molecule have more than one type of bond?
faq.a: Yes, molecules often have different types of bonds connecting different atoms. For example, a molecule might have both single and double bonds. You could also ask: 'Can bonds mix?' or 'Does one molecule have different bonds?'
asks: Can I have a molecule with different bonds?
Is it possible to have single and double bonds together?

facts: Covalent bonds involve the sharing of valence electrons between atoms.
A single bond represents one shared pair of electrons.
A double bond represents two shared pairs of electrons.
A triple bond represents three shared pairs of electrons.
